nameStory: The "sticky" in Sticky Catchfly comes from the plant's remarkable superpower - its stems are covered in a gluey substance just below each leaf joint that traps small insects like natural flypaper! The Latin name Viscaria literally means "sticky," and "catchfly" refers to how flies and other tiny bugs get caught on these tacky spots. It's like nature's own bug trap, built right into the plant!
description: Sticky Catchfly is an upright perennial wildflower that grows up to 2 feet tall, producing eye-catching spikes of bright rosy-pink flowers. This member of the pink family has narrow, lance-shaped leaves and a distinctive sticky coating on its stems that gives it both its name and its bug-catching ability. The cheerful pink blooms appear in whorled clusters along tall spikes, making it a standout wildflower when you spot it growing on rocky cliffs and slopes. Though rare in New England with only a few recorded sightings, it's an exciting find for nature explorers!

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel the stem just below where leaves attach - it's noticeably sticky and tacky to the touch, like natural glue that may have tiny insects stuck to it

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright rosy-pink flowers about 3/4 inch across arranged in long, whorled spikes that bloom from May through August

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that taper to points, arranged opposite each other along the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial growing 1-2 feet tall with multiple flower spikes rising from the base, forming small colonies in rocky areas

habitat: Look for Sticky Catchfly in rocky, well-drained locations like cliff faces, rocky outcrops, and stony slopes throughout New England. It thrives in areas with thin soil and good drainage, often growing in crevices between rocks or on exposed ledges. This hardy wildflower prefers open, sunny spots where few other plants can establish themselves.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the base with fresh lance-shaped leaves. Early flowers may begin appearing in late May.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright pink flower spikes most visible from June through August. The sticky stems are most noticeable during active growth.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop. Leaves may begin to yellow and die back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level as a perennial, leaving only the root system alive underground until spring regrowth.

funFact: This plant is basically a living bug motel - the sticky stems don't just accidentally trap insects, they actually provide the plant with extra nutrition when the trapped bugs decompose, making Sticky Catchfly a part-time carnivorous plant!
confusionNotes: The bright pink flowers might be confused with other members of the pink family, but no other New England wildflower has that distinctive sticky, tacky feeling on the stems. If you can't feel the "glue" just below the leaf joints, it's not a Sticky Catchfly!
contextualKnowledge: In botanical references, you might see this plant listed as Lychnis viscaria, which is an older scientific name that's still commonly used in gardening circles. Both names refer to the same sticky-stemmed wildflower, so don't be confused if you see it called by either name.
compareHints: Since Sticky Catchfly is the only Viscaria species in our region, compare it to other pink family members like Wild Pink or Fire Pink. Unlike these relatives, Sticky Catchfly has that unmistakable tacky coating on its stems and grows in distinctly whorled flower clusters rather than loose, branching flower heads. The sticky stem feature is unique among New England's pink family members.
